sources.cite: AWS Big Data Blog, 'Detect and handle data skew on AWS Glue'
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: 'You can use the Spark UI to identify which tasks are taking longer to complete than others'; with skew 'you will see very biased values in each percentile'; the observability metrics glue.driver.skewness.job and glue.driver.skewness.stage; a job that 'doesn't scale with the number of workers' is a symptom; Glue 4.0 (Spark 3.3) enables Adaptive Query Execution by default; salting 'involves adding a random prefix to the key of skewed data'. Splitting out a placeholder key before a join is the author's applied example (general Spark practice, to verify against the Spark tuning guide).

brief.situation: You are the on-call data engineer at Quillon Outfitters, a fictional retailer. The nightly Glue job orders-enrich joins the day's orders with the customer table and normally takes about 40 minutes from 02:00. Today it is still running at 05:00. Finance's extract reads its output at 06:00.
handover: Two days ago the web shop launched guest checkout; guest orders carry customer_id 'GUEST'.
The job runs on Glue 4.0 with 10 G.1X workers; yesterday's output is still in the curated bucket.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the Glue job's stages, the skewed key and the finance extract that waits for the output.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: why the job ran three hours, what you changed, and how it stays fixed.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Connects one slow task to one key.
parts.modelAnswer: In the join stage 199 tasks took under a minute and one read 61 GB; 38% of today's orders carry customer_id 'GUEST' since guest checkout launched, and a join sends all rows with one key to one task.

parts.label: What
parts.criteria: Removes the skew instead of adding capacity.
parts.modelAnswer: Stopped the run and re-ran with GUEST rows kept out of the join and unioned back with empty customer fields; it finished in 34 minutes. More workers would have idled, and copying yesterday's output would have published wrong numbers.

parts.label: Stays fixed
parts.criteria: Code, alarm and the source team.
parts.modelAnswer: The split is in the job's code, an alarm watches glue.driver.skewness.job, and the checkout team has a ticket to announce placeholder keys before launch.

expertPath.text: Spark UI: one task 2h40m, 61 GB; top key GUEST 38%; skewness 31.8; run time tripled since the guest launch.
Stop and re-run with GUEST split out; commit the split, skew alarm, ticket to checkout.

staleData.headline: A late report beats a wrong one
staleData.body: Copying old output under a new date produces numbers nobody can tell are wrong. If the run cannot finish, tell finance it is late.

extractMissed.headline: Skew does not yield to more workers
extractMissed.body: One key in 38% of the rows puts them all in one task. Split that key out of the join (or salt it); more workers only add idle ones.

unskewed.headline: Good: found the key, not more workers
unskewed.body: You read the task distribution, found the one key behind it, split it out of the join, confirmed the run finished, and made the fix permanent with an alarm.

gaps.headline: Held, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria show what was left: the evidence before the change, the lasting step, the check, or the cause in the record.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: One task out of 200 is still running after hours and has read 61 GB while the rest finished in under a minute: that is skew, and the key query shows why, 38% of the orders carry 'GUEST' since guest checkout launched. More workers cannot split one key's rows. Keep the placeholder key out of the join and add those rows back after, re-run, and check the output; then make it permanent with a skew alarm. Copying yesterday's output would publish wrong numbers.
